CREST actor journeys
Overview — what CREST is and who is involved
CREST · ROLES + HAPPY PATHS

Every actor in CREST, and what each one actually does

CREST is digital public infrastructure for verifiable work history. It gives an informal worker a portable, cryptographically verifiable record of what they have done, who they worked for, and what they are capable of. The record belongs to the worker and travels with them across employers, campaigns and countries.

Delivering that takes 34 distinct roles. This walkthrough shows them in four layers: first the structure — who assigns whom, and how the categories relate; then the happy paths — the eight end-to-end flows that make up CREST in operation; then the individual journeys — screen-by-screen for the roles where a detailed layer is drawn today, and a role card for every other role; and finally the open points that are still to be decided. Twenty-five automated system services are named beside the screens where they act.

The atomic unit

A work unit: a verifiable record of a discrete piece of work, attested by an issuer under a work definition published by a work definition author, owned by the worker, presentable to any verifier.

Work units accumulate into a credential history. That history becomes the basis for skill recognition, hiring and access to finance. Payment is the first use case that makes credentials immediately valuable — not the purpose of the system.

What it is not
A payments system
It configures a rate and tracks movement. It never holds or moves money.
A matching engine
It supplies the validated inputs. Someone else builds the marketplace.
A credit scorer
A lender can use the history. CREST does not score workers.
A surveillance system
Verifiers see only what a worker consents to. Raw location is never stored.
One mandatory workflow
A project composes only the parts it needs.
THREE TIERS OF ATTESTATION

The tier is a visible property of every credential, not backend metadata. All three are valid. Without the distinction, 200 self-asserted events look identical to 200 outcome-validated ones until a verifier is deceived.

Tier 1Outcome-linked

Strongest — recorded independently by a service delivery system

Primary risk: Identity mapping errors; source data quality

Tier 2Supervisor-entered

Medium — the issuer has authority but also bias

Primary risk: Supervisor-worker collusion or coercion

Tier 3Worker-asserted

Weakest — no corroboration, and essential for inclusion

Primary risk: Inflation of work history

1 · THE MODEL

Three levels, and what each participant needs

L1 · InfrastructureL2 · ConfigurationL3 · ProductEvery screen in the Screens tab carries the level it belongs to.

CREST is described in three layers. What must be true everywhere, what a project sets for itself, and what somebody happens to have built on top. Almost every argument about this product turns out to be about which layer something belongs in.

L1 · Infrastructure
Objects, registries and the rules that cannot bend. True in every deployment, for a decade.
L2 · Configuration
How a deployment — and far more often one project — expresses its own reality, as data.
L3 · Product
Everything on the Screens tab. A deployment may replace all of it and still be CREST.
L1 · Infrastructure
What must be true in every deployment, in every country, for a decade. Objects, registries, and the rules that cannot bend. Changes slowly and by consensus.
L2 · Configuration
How a deployment — and far more often an individual project — expresses its own reality, as data. Two projects side by side may look almost nothing alike. This is where adoption is won.
L3 · Product
Apps, journeys, dashboards, and the personas they were designed for. Everything on the Screens tab. A deployment may replace all of it and still be CREST.

The test: if two deployments could reasonably disagree about it and both still be CREST, it is not infrastructure.

What the worker needs

Everything else in this model exists to make these true. They are stated as the worker would state them, because that is the only way to tell whether they are met.

What must be true
Why it cannot bend
W1
I can exist here without a document, without a phone, and without being able to read
Requiring any of the three excludes exactly the people this is for
W2
Someone can register me on my behalf, and it counts the same
Assisted enrolment is a first-class path, not a fallback
W3
My work is recorded whether or not I hold a device
The device is the employer’s problem, not mine
W4
Next campaign, I am found — I do not start again
Re-enrolment is how a history gets fragmented
W5
I can see what I have done, what was accepted, and what I am owed
Otherwise the record is about me but not for me
W6
If something is sent back, I am told, and told why
Silence is how a worker quietly loses money
W7
I can show my work to a stranger in under a minute, with no signal
A hiring desk will not wait, and there is often no network
W8
Showing it does not hand over my name, my number or where I live
Proving capability and surrendering identity are different acts
W9
I keep everything when the employer ends
This is the whole point of the system
W10
If something is wrong, a person I can reach looks at it
Not a queue three levels away

The problems this exists for

Stated plainly, per actor. Every object in the model traces back to one of these.

Actor
What is wrong today
Worker
Work leaves no record they hold. They cannot prove it to another programme, in another district or another country. When their record is questioned they have nothing to show. They are re-registered each campaign, asked for documents they do not have, told a payment is coming with no way to check, and not told why something was rejected.
Project
Every project builds its own set-up and buys its own tools. Identifying a worker costs money every time. Validating work costs money every time. The same fact is needed at different moments for different reasons — whom to employ, whom to train, what was delivered, who to pay — and each is answered separately. Work validated once cannot be relied on by the next project.
Funder
Reported figures on work done and funds used cannot easily be trusted. They arrive late and in the reporter’s shape. Different information is needed at different points, and each request costs the project weeks. Aggregates cannot be traced back. Money reported as spent cannot be tied to work reported as done.
Person checking
No way to tell a real claim from a made-up one, and no way to check a body they have never heard of. Needs an answer in the moment, often with no signal. Asking for proof usually means asking for identity documents they have no right to hold.

A unit of work exists on its own

The change that matters most in this version. A household was visited, a round was completed, a session was held — that happened, and it is a record in its own right. A claim is a separate assertion that a particular worker did it.

Why they are separate
A project can count what was delivered without resolving who delivered it. A unit can serve a purpose other than crediting a worker — measuring a facility’s throughput, evidencing output, paying a team. And a disputed claim does not destroy the record that the work happened; what is contested is who did it.
What follows
One unit may carry one claim, none, or several where more than one person worked on it. The unit is what a definition measures; the claim is what a credential is about.

What is kept, and by whom

Ten registries. A registry is the whole set of one kind of record, with somebody answerable for it — rules about one record sit on the record, rules about the whole set sit here. No two workers are the same person cannot be checked from inside a single worker record.

There is deliberately no register of credentials
Credentials are listed centrally nowhere. That is a privacy property rather than an omission, and it is why a separate withdrawal mechanism exists as the single central fact about them — it carries whether a credential still stands, and nothing else.
Most attestation has no human in it
A claim can be vouched for by a named person, or inferred from a source system’s own record with nobody acting at all. The second is the majority at scale, and it is why strength is worked out rather than declared.
Strength is never stored
It is resolved at the moment somebody asks, from where the record came, how it was captured, and what the definition required. Writing it onto the record would freeze a judgement that should move when a definition is versioned or a source is re-assessed.
Consent happens three times
Once at enrolment, covering the right to fetch and hold. Again before each credential exists, when the worker confirms the draft is right. And again at every disclosure. Only the third is about who may see; the second is about whether the record is true.
Offline means QR or NFC
A worker’s proof is readable with no signal, by a scanned code or by a tap where the device supports it. Both carry the same payload and neither needs the issuer to be reachable.

One decision still open

How organisations are brought in, and who vouches for them
Three options, and everything else works under any of them. Administrative — the deployment creates organisations itself; cheapest, and breaks when a partner arrives the state did not create. Self-registration and approval — an organisation registers, requests terms, and is approved; scales to bodies nobody anticipated. This is what every screen now draws. The word the screens use for a policy is “terms”: one object, read by an organisation and held in the registry. Delegated accreditation — an accredited organisation may vouch for others, forming a chain a verifier walks; richest and much the most expensive.

What decides it: whether an unfamiliar verifier needs to know which organisation stood behind the work, or only which country. The first two can run on a single signing key held by the deployment, which removes the key-custody problem entirely. Only the third needs distributed signing.
What these screens assume
Everything on the Screens tab draws the second option — an organisation registers itself, chooses published terms, and is approved. That is an assumption made so there is something to look at, not a decision.

The PRD now sets out five options rather than three, and every journey draws one of them: self-registration where the organisation’s registration number is checked against a national register, with a person deciding only where that check cannot be made. The recognition screens that used to show organisations being endorsed and granted a status have gone. Nothing grants a status and no organisation vouches for another. Joining a project is a separate act and is drawn the same way throughout: the project invites, the grant is narrower than the organisation’s terms in function, place and period, and it cannot be passed on.
2 · HAPPY PATHS

How CREST works, end to end

Nine flows, drawn as swimlanes. Each role journey on the Screens tab links to the one it belongs to. Each shows who does what, in what order, and where a handoff happens. Click any role at the foot of a diagram to open its screens.

Diagram 1 of 9

1. Setting up a deployment, and how organisations arrive

One country, one deployment. An organisation registers itself — it is not invited — and what it may do comes from a published set of terms, not a negotiation.

Diagram 2 of 9

2. Setting up a project

A project exists after two answers. Everything else is a checklist, and each outstanding item states what it blocks.

Diagram 3 of 9

3. Defining the work, and where its evidence comes from

What counts as done, versioned. The evidence source is declared here, and it caps how strongly anything can ever be evidenced.

Diagram 4 of 9

4. Registering a worker, either way

A worker exists on a name and one contact route. No document, no phone, no reading required — and an assisted registration counts exactly the same.

Diagram 5 of 9

5. From work done to something the worker holds

Evidence arrives from a system the worker may never touch. How it was captured decides how strongly it can ever be evidenced.

Diagram 6 of 9

6. Paying for work that was accepted

Payment is optional. A definition is complete and usable with no rate attached, because recognition and credentialing are uses of their own.

Diagram 7 of 9

7. When a worker says something is wrong

A worker must be able to reach a person who knows their project — not a queue three levels away.

Diagram 8 of 9

8. Checking that the money actually landed

What was instructed against what was confirmed. Every unmatched amount resolves to one reason with one owner.

Diagram 9 of 9

9. Reading a worker’s wallet, with and without consent

What a stranger sees the moment they scan, and what changes only if the worker agrees. Showing the code is itself the consent for the first part — nothing identifying is in it.

3 · ROLES AND PERSONAS

Eleven roles, thirty-three personas

A role is a named set of permissions somebody holds. A persona is a person the product was designed for. The old list of thirty-four mixed the two, which is why it kept growing — every new person in a journey minted a new role, even where the permissions already existed.

Three an organisation holds

Type
What its terms cover
Delivery
Registers workers · defines work where its terms carry it · submits work units · reviews · connects its own source systems
Payment
Configures a pathway · executes disbursement · reconciles
Verifying
Reads the record behind a credential, where a worker consents

Eight a person holds, inside it

Role
What it covers
Administrator
Assigns people, sets the organisation’s configuration, accepts project invitations
Author
Drafts work definitions, rates and payment set-up — where the terms carry define-work
Approver
Ratifies what an author drafted, and may never draft it
Operator
Registers, attests, submits work units and claims, validates, executes
Reviewer
Reads a project or a portfolio. Never a write on what is reviewed
Support
Resolves a worker’s problem. A project cannot activate without one
Verifier
Checks a credential, and reads the record behind it where the worker consents
Worker
Sees their own record, claims work, decides what is shared
A funder holds two roles, on purpose
Reviewer shows a portfolio in aggregate. Verifier is what lets any of it be traced to the work behind it. Aggregate oversight and individual inspection are different acts with different consequences for the worker, so they are different roles and granted separately.

Three personas hold no role at all. Two are acts of commitment rather than permissions, and one — the person who checks a credential with a pass — has no account to hold anything with.

THE SCREENS

Twelve journeys, end to end

Each journey is a run somebody actually lives through, drawn screen by screen with the reasoning beside every screen. Click a role to walk it.

1
Onboarding an organisation
Key actor: Onboarding Authorising Signatory · 13 screens

Four fields and two questions to exist. Then, separately and only when needed: documents to earn a status, and an invitation to work on a project. Identify, qualify, enable — three moments, three clocks, never collapsed into one form.

2
Setting up the instance
Key actor: Instance Administrator · 9 screens

One person establishes the deployment, sets the consent rules, and admits the first organisation.

3
Setting up a project
Key actor: Project Configurator · 16 screens

An organisation puts people into roles, creates a project, and decides what that project needs from CREST.

4
Defining the work
Key actor: Work Definition Author · 27 screens

What counts as done, what proves it, who checks it, and — separately — what it pays.

5
Payment, and putting it right
Key actor: Rate Owner and Payment Mechanism Owner · 15 screens

Setting what the work pays, choosing how the money reaches the worker, and connecting the rail that moves it.

6
Registering a worker who cannot self-register
Key actor: Registering Agent · 5 screens

Enrollment in the field, offline, with consent recorded as voice and a card printed on the spot.

7
A worker, end to end
Key actor: Worker · 22 screens

Registration through to a credential in hand and a payment received.

8
From attestation to credential
Key actor: Supervisor (Attestor) · 8 screens

A supervisor confirms work happened. Acceptance of the evidence is what issues the credential — no person signs it.

9
Checking a credential
Key actor: Verifier · 6 screens

Two kinds of third party. One takes a self-service pass and sees yes-or-no. The other is onboarded to the registry and sees more — but never more than the worker allowed.

10
When something stalls
Key actor: Support Agent · 6 screens

A registration or payment that did not complete, and what can be explained rather than escalated.

11
Seeing where it stands
Key actor: Project Configurator, funder, registry custodian · 12 screens

Dashboards built to change behaviour rather than to report. Straight-through rate with ranked causes and an owner each, tier quality split into capped-by-source versus fell-short, payment delay as a taxonomy including one reason owned by nobody, and registry coverage measured as payable rather than registered.

12
Systems CREST does not own
Key actor: External systems · 4 screens

The identity service, the platform where evidence originates, the payment rail, and a next employer checking a credential.

The first screen anyone ever sees

On screen: Instance Administrator — new deployment

Nothing in CREST can exist before an instance does. This is the only screen in the entire system that renders against an empty database, and the only act that is self-authorised — there is nobody above the Instance Administrator to grant it.

Why it works this way

The roles master is explicit that G-1 is self-established at instance stand-up. Every other authority in the instance is eventually traceable back to a decision made on this screen and the three that follow it.

Assumption — accept or reject

The four-step checklist is my proposal. The roles master states the ordering constraint (consent rules before the first worker; recognition before the first organisation) but does not say the operator is walked through it as a guided sequence rather than a settings area they explore.

Naming the instance, and binding identity

On screen: Instance Administrator — Kenya, National

An instance is scoped to a jurisdiction and bound to whichever identity system that jurisdiction already runs. CREST never creates identity; it binds to an anchor and links everything afterwards.

Why it works this way

Data residency and the identity anchor are the two decisions that cannot be revisited cheaply. Putting them on the first configuration screen, rather than in a settings area, makes that visible while the instance is still empty.

Assumption — accept or reject

The language list is mine. Nothing in the architecture requires a worker-facing language set to be declared at instance level — it could equally be per project. Declaring it here makes it a property of the deployment rather than something each project can quietly skip.

Consent rules, before the first worker

These are set once for the instance and inherited by every project. A project can be stricter; it cannot be looser.

A worker may withdraw consent at any time
Withdrawal stops future disclosure. It does not delete credentials already issued.
A worker may see every verification of their own record
Who checked, when, and what they were shown.
Disclosure is per share, never standing
A verifier gets one scoped view, not an open account.
Projects may request a broader default
Off. Leaving this off means no project can widen disclosure below the instance rule.
Data Protection / Consent Officer
Not yet appointed
This role owns these rules from here on. Instance Administrator sets them; Data Protection / Consent Officer maintains them.
Set before the first worker registers, deliberately. Retro-fitting consent onto records already collected under a different rule has no clean answer.
L1 · InfrastructureInstance Administrator Administrator · the operating organisationOne console · instance viewInherited by every project

Consent rules come before the first worker

On screen: Instance Administrator → Data Protection Officer (G-3)

The instance sets a consent floor that every project inherits. A project may be stricter than the instance; it can never be looser. The Data Protection Officer maintains these rules afterwards.

Why it works this way

The roles master places G-3 early on purpose: consent rules should exist before the first worker registers, not be added afterwards. A record collected under one rule and read under another is the problem this ordering avoids.

Assumption — accept or reject

The four specific rules are my proposal, not a specification. What the architecture establishes is that consent is a gate enforced at share time; which defaults an instance ships with, and whether a project can request a broader one at all, is an open policy decision.

What the system does here
S-12
Consent Management & Access Control Service
Is configured here. Every later disclosure is checked against what this screen sets.

The invitation names a person

On screen: Instance Administrator → Onboarding Authorising Signatory (G-2)

The invitation goes to a named senior officer who can commit their organisation. CREST cannot appoint an organisation’s own signatory, so this is an invitation to self-identify, not an assignment.

Why it works this way

G-2 is the one role in the governance chain that is self-appointed, because only the organisation can say who is empowered to bind it. Everything downstream of that organisation traces authority back to whoever accepts here.

Assumption — accept or reject

The domain check against existing organisations is a simplified stand-in. Real root-uniqueness — making sure two entities cannot both claim to be the same ministry — is an open question, not something a domain comparison settles.

Services, not roles

On screen: Instance Administrator · platform services board

These are actions the platform performs, not people. They are grouped by stage and shown by state, because the useful question for an operator is which parts of the system are actually live for this deployment.

Why it works this way

Payment being idle rather than absent is the point. Compositability means a project can adopt the trust layer alone, and nothing in the credential path should depend on a payment component being present or connected.

Assumption — accept or reject

A services board of this shape is my proposal. The roles master lists the twenty-five services and names X-1 as their accountable owner, but does not describe an operator-facing view of them, or say what an operator can actually do when one is unhealthy.

What is not here
Verifiers are not in this queue and never will be. Any third party can verify a credential without onboarding — the credential’s signature carries the trust, not the verifier’s status.
Why the queue is short
Requests where the register confirms the organisation are approved automatically and never reach this screen. Registration itself is not in the queue at all, because an organisation is listed and findable the moment it registers.
L1 · Infrastructure Administrator · the operating organisation One console · instance view

A queue of exceptions, not of everybody

On screen: Instance Administrator

A request whose registration number the register confirms is approved without anybody seeing it. What lands here is the remainder: a number that does not match, a register that was unreachable, or a kind of body no register in the country covers. Nothing is graded and no status is granted, and the only outcome is that the requested terms are approved or returned with a reason.

Why it works this way

A person reading a scanned certificate cannot be held to a turnaround time and cannot be audited afterwards, which is why the register does the check wherever it can. What is left is a queue small enough for one person to run, made of cases that genuinely need judgement rather than of every organisation that ever applied.

Open — not decided

A turnaround time is now achievable and still unstated. Community-based organisations are the real gap: no register covers many of them, so they land here permanently rather than occasionally, which is the case for requiring a sponsor instead.

L1 · Infrastructure Administrator · the operating organisation One console · instance view

What can actually be checked, and what cannot

On screen: Instance Administrator

This request is here because the register did not confirm it. Everything the terms require is present, and the one check that would have approved this automatically is the one that failed, so it is shown as failed rather than quietly passed.

Why it works this way

Approval is the moment an organisation’s connection begins, and from then on anything its systems send is accepted. When the register cannot settle it, somebody is deciding on weaker evidence than usual, and the screen says so rather than presenting five green ticks.

Open — not decided

What an approver should demand when the register fails is undefined. A ministry with an unreachable register and a body no register covers are very different cases arriving on the same screen, and nothing distinguishes them.

Approving the request

One decision, and it grants exactly what the published terms say. There is no higher or lower version of being approved.

Full delivery with payment, version 3requested
Enrol workers, say what work is, send records, validate, set rates and move money. Four organisations are on these terms today.
✓
Puts this organisation on version 3, as published
Not a copy, and not amended for them. If version 4 is published later, they stay on 3 until they ask.
✓
Issues one key, shown once
Nothing they send would have been accepted before this moment, however correctly it was formed.
✓
Grants nothing beyond those terms
A project may later give them less than the terms allow. It can never give them more.
✓
Creates no status, and no authority over anybody else
They cannot vouch for another organisation, because nothing in this deployment works that way.
If it is ever withdrawn
A withdrawn key is never reinstated — a new one is issued instead. There is no middle state in which an organisation is technically able to send but not permitted to.
What happens next
Who acts next: nobody, necessarily. An approved organisation sits in the directory until a project configurator goes looking for a partner like it. That may be tomorrow or never, and either is a normal state.
L1 · Infrastructure Administrator · the operating organisation One console · instance view

Approval is the whole decision

On screen: Instance Administrator

Approving a request puts the organisation on the exact version of the terms it read, and mints the key that makes its connection real. Those two things happen together, on purpose.

Why it works this way

Keeping the terms and the connection as one gate rather than two means there is never a state where an organisation is permitted but unable, or able but not permitted. It also means an approver is never deciding how much to trust somebody. They are deciding whether the required documents are present for a set of terms somebody else published.

Open — not decided

Nothing yet decides what happens to records already in flight when a key is withdrawn.

What you can do here
Approve and issue the key
The organisation sees its key once, on its own screen
Back
Returns to the submission

Data Protection / Consent Officer

Instance
DEFINITION ONLY — SCREENS NOT DRAWN

Sets consent and personal-data rules for the instance.

Sets the rules for how the instance handles worker consent and personal data, and how a worker can see, correct, or revoke access to their own history. Placed early because consent rules should exist before the first worker registers, not be added later. G-4

Worker Registry Custodian

Instance
Step 1 of 4
New journeyJourney 12 of 12Minding the registry

The accountable custodian of the worker registry. Two things flow through this role: routine writes (accepting every new worker record, update, or merge originated by a Registering Agent or a self-registration flow) and judgment calls (resolving flagged duplicates and any override to the automated identity flow). Both are worker-registry write authority; kept as one role rather than split into two. Registering Agent (W-2) captures the data; the Worker Registry Custodian (G-4) accepts the write — that split preserves segregation of duties. Held by the deployment operator, and not tied to any other organisation existing first.

G-6

Accrediting Authority

Delivery Org
NOT PRESENT UNDER THE OPTION THIS PROTOTYPE DRAWS

In an organisation that holds accrediting rights, grants, limits or revokes the standing of organisations beneath it in the trust chain, and issues each one its accreditation credential.

In an organisation that holds accrediting rights, grants, limits or revokes the standing of organisations beneath it in the trust chain, and issues each one its accreditation credential. Authority to issue therefore travels down the chain rather than being handed out centrally: a campaign coordinator can issue because a district authorised them, which derives from a province, which derives from the root. Every hop is a signed accreditation, so a verifier can trace any credential back to the root without asking anyone. The same authority at every level, not a different role per tier. In the first deployment it instantiates as ministry, then province, then district, then facility, then campaign coordinator — but nothing in the role assumes health, so it works unchanged for sanitation, construction or delivery. The Instance Administrator (G-1) still admits the first organisation; after that, accreditation is delegable.

What this project needs from CREST

Five independent choices. None is a degraded version of another, and a project that answers no to most of them is still a valid project.

Register workers
Run CREST enrollment, or map identifiers from a registry you already have.
Define work
What counts as done, what proves it, who checks it.
Set up payment
Configure a rate and decide how the money reaches the worker. Off means credentials still issue, with no rate attached.
Validate
Check evidence received from another system, or uploaded as a spreadsheet, against the definition before a credential issues. CREST never records the work itself.
Carry forward
A worker keeps their verified history after this project ends.
A project with a mature worker registry and its own bank relationship can adopt the trust layer alone — register off, pay off, validate on. The credential is never contingent on a payment component being present, connected or resolved.

Five choices, answered separately

On screen: Project Configurator — Malaria Bednet Campaign

This is the screen compositability actually lives on. Each capability is answered on its own, and turning one off narrows what the project does without weakening what it still produces.

Why it works this way

The architecture is explicit that a credential must never be contingent on a payment component. Presenting these as five independent switches, rather than a tier or a plan, is what keeps that promise visible to whoever is configuring.

Assumption — accept or reject

Presenting all five on one screen is my proposal. The roles master lists the choices a Project Configurator makes but does not group them this way, and does not say whether a capability can be switched off again once a project has live workers.

Where the workers come from

Register them here, bring in records that already exist, or both. Both is common: a registry covers the known workers, enrollment covers the rest.

Register in CREST
Full enrollment — identity, consent, recovery contacts. Self-registration or assisted by a Registering Agent.
Import existing records
Map identifiers from a registry you already run onto Crest identities. Nobody is re-registered.
Import only
No enrollment at all. Every worker must already exist in the source registry.
Source registry
Kenya CHW Registry — 14,200 records
Whoever operates it holds Source-System Administrator (Source-System Administrator), and is accountable if a record there is wrong or stale.
Importing does not create identities. It links an existing identifier to a Crest identity, so a worker already known to the county is not enrolled a second time under a new number.
L2 · ConfigurationProject Configurator Administrator · one projectOne console · project viewChoice one of three

Registration and import are not alternatives

On screen: Project Configurator — worker sourcing

A project can register fresh, import what already exists, or do both. Import is not a lesser path — for an organisation with a real registry it is the correct one, and re-enrolling those workers would create duplicates rather than value.

Why it works this way

Identity is created once and linked every time after. Import exists so that an organisation with its own registry never has to break that rule, and so accountability for a stale record stays with whoever operates the source system.

Assumption — accept or reject

Offering all three as explicit options is my proposal. The architecture establishes that both paths exist; it does not say a project picks between them on a configuration screen, or what happens when an imported worker later tries to self-register.

How does evidence reach CREST?

CREST does not record work. Somewhere else already does, and this decides how that record gets here. Both options can run at once, on different definitions.

A system CREST pulls from
An adaptor reads records on a schedule from a platform that already logs the work: a campaign system, a case-management tool, an HR or attendance system. Nobody retypes anything, and nobody in the chain had a reason to change the number.
A spreadsheet the project uploads
CREST generates a template from the work definition. Whoever holds the records fills it and the project uploads it. A person opened the file and typed into it, so it is weaker evidence than a system record, however careful they were.
Somebody entering work into CRESTnot available
This does not exist and will not be built. A record CREST captured itself would be evidence CREST is vouching for on its own authority, which is the one thing the trust model cannot do.
Why both, usually
The two are not alternatives, and most real projects need both. A campaign system covers the work it manages, and there is always work it does not: a training an institute ran, a round a contractor completed, a month a partner recorded on paper.
Pull from
DIGIT HCM · Kisumu instance  ▾
How often
Nightly, 02:00  ▾
Upload accepted from
The Org Admin of any organisation on this project  ▾
Whoever uploads is recorded on every row the file produces
L2 · ConfigurationProject Configurator Administrator · one projectOne console · project view

Two ways in, and there is no third

On screen: Project Configurator

This is the screen that says CREST is downstream of everything. Work is recorded where it is recorded, and this decides whether CREST reads it from a system or receives it as a file. Entering work into CREST is shown as unavailable rather than left out, so nobody wonders whether it is hidden somewhere.

Why it works this way

The tier hierarchy is entirely about who had the opportunity to change the number. A system that logged a delivery for its own reasons had none, which is what makes its record the strongest thing available. Once a person has opened a spreadsheet, that is no longer true, and the strength drops accordingly. If CREST captured the record itself there would be nobody independent left in the chain, and the credential would be asserting its own evidence.

Open — not decided

Nothing decides what happens when the same work arrives twice, once pulled and once in an uploaded file. Deduplication is named nowhere in this product.

What the check actually is
Every row is checked against WD-4471 v1.2 before anything is accepted: does the worker exist, is the definition the active version, is the quantity within what the definition permits, is the date inside the period, is the place inside the grant. A row that fails any of those is held, and the rest are unaffected.
L2 · ConfigurationProject Configurator Administrator · one projectOne console · project view

The file is checked against the definition, row by row

On screen: Project Configurator

A spreadsheet is the second of the two ways in, and it is the one a project will actually use in the first month. The template came from the work definition, so the check is not a guess about what the columns mean. Six of three hundred and twelve rows do not match, and the other three hundred and six are not held up waiting for them.

Why it works this way

Rejecting a whole file because six rows are wrong is how a month of work stops moving, and accepting all of it because most rows are fine is how a definition stops meaning anything. Holding exactly the rows that failed is the only behaviour that does not force a choice between those two.

Open — not decided

Whether a held row can be corrected in place, or has to be resubmitted in a new file, is undecided. Correcting in place is easier and puts a person back inside the evidence path, which is what the tier ceiling exists to price.

Payment, calculation only, or neither

Three genuinely different postures. The third is not a failure state.

Track money movement
CREST calculates what is owed and follows the instruction through to confirmation on a rail.
Calculation only
CREST produces a versioned statement of what is owed. Somebody else pays it, outside CREST entirely.
No rate at all
Credentials issue with no payment attached. Used where the value is recognition or credentialing.
Pay rate
Set separately — not part of ratifying the definition
A Work Definition must be complete and usable with no pay information attached.
Manual payment approval
Off
On would send every payment to a Payment Approver (Payment Mechanism Owner) before release.
Pay rate is a separate object from the work definition, deliberately. Payment is one CREST use case among several, and a definition can never be gated on deciding whether anyone gets paid.
L2 · ConfigurationProject Configurator Administrator · one projectOne console · project viewChoice two of three

Payment is a posture, not a feature flag

On screen: Project Configurator — payment integration

Three postures that produce genuinely different systems: one that follows money to confirmation, one that only says what is owed, and one with no rate at all. All three issue the same credentials.

Why it works this way

Payment is the first use case that makes credentials immediately valuable, not the purpose of the system. Keeping the rate a separate object from the definition is what lets a recognition-only or credentialing-only project exist without pretending to be a payment project with the numbers left blank.

Assumption — accept or reject

The three-way framing is my proposal. The architecture establishes payment integration, advisory, or neither as a real choice; the specific wording and the placement of the manual-approval switch on this screen are mine.

Wakes only under the first two options, and only once a rate exists.

Runs under the first option only — there is no status to track if CREST never issues an instruction.

Configuring a project is not staffing it

On screen: Project Configurator — project roles

The configuration is done; the project still cannot run. These five roles have to be held by named people who have accepted, and each of them can be a different person in a different department.

Why it works this way

The separation of Rate Owner from Payment Mechanism Owner is the one worth pausing on. How much a worker is owed and how the money physically reaches them are separate decisions, and the roles master keeps them apart rather than collapsing them into a finance role.

Assumption — accept or reject

Sending all five invitations from one screen is my proposal. The roles master says each is assigned by the Org Admin; whether the Project Configurator can originate those invitations for their own project, or only request them, is not specified.

What happens on 31 March
The grant lapses on 31 March by itself. Work validated before then stays validated and every credential already issued is untouched, because what ends is permission to do more rather than the standing of what was already done. Anything still unvalidated on that date becomes a named handoff rather than disappearing.
What Amref cannot do with this
This grant cannot be passed on. If Amref sub-contracts two sub-counties, those bodies are invited by this project directly and hold their own grants. Amref cannot bring them in.
L2 · ConfigurationProject Configurator Administrator · one projectOne console · project view

The grant is narrower than the terms, and it ends

On screen: Project Configurator

Three things are decided here and none of them is who the organisation is. Which of their capabilities apply on this project, which definitions and which places they apply to, and between which dates. A capability their terms do not carry is shown and cannot be selected.

Why it works this way

Two different bodies are making two different decisions, and neither can stand in for the other. The deployment approved the terms once, centrally, and that is a ceiling nobody on this screen can raise. The project owns the workers, the evidence and the records, so the project decides who touches them. Showing the ungrantable capability rather than hiding it is what makes the ceiling legible instead of mysterious.

Open — not decided

Whether a grant can be narrowed after it is live, and whether doing so affects work already submitted under it, is undecided. Widening is clear: it needs a new invitation.

Support belongs to the project, not the platform

On screen: Project Configurator

The first point of contact for any worker on this project is a named person inside this project, staffed and budgeted by it. The platform handles only what a project structurally cannot.

Why it works this way

A worker whose payment has not arrived does not have a platform problem. They have a problem with this project, whose staff know the work, the supervisors and the pay cycle. Routing them to a central queue three levels away turns a ten-minute fix into a three-week silence — and the project that caused the problem never learns it happened.

Open — not decided

L2 · Configuration Project Configurator Administrator · one project Web console

Two things a funder always wants, pre-built

On screen: Project Configurator

Fund utilisation reconciled stage by stage, and proof of work with the tier mix included. Self-serve, saveable, schedulable, shareable so the funder can re-run it.

Why it works this way

Funder reporting is where projects lose weeks, because every funder wants the same facts arranged differently. Fixing the facts and making the arrangement configurable turns a data request into a report. Including the tier mix is what makes it proof rather than a claim.

Open — not decided

Nothing constrains what a saved report may expose. Individual-level cuts are off by default here, but no governance rule prevents somebody enabling them.

What you can do here

Runs against live data without saving
Save and share
The funder re-runs it themselves

Monthly, to a named recipient

Defines, reuses, versions, or clones a Work Definition, including its evidence-tier rules; requests or adapts a template. Also sets its issuance policy — which evidence tiers issue a credential automatically, what the credential asserts, and which organisations are authorised to issue against this definition (authorised_issuers[]). Those organisations become the credential's issuer; the definition never names a person.

The registry of work definitions

On screen: Work Definition Author — "Define work" on screen

Every definition this institution has authored, with its version and status. Definitions are immutable once ACTIVE — a change publishes a new version rather than editing the record.

Why it works this way

The word "Work Definition Author" appears nowhere on screen. It is the correct term in the schema and in field names like work definition author_did, but the interface says "Define work" because a non-technical author should not have to learn a piece of architecture vocabulary to do their job.

Assumption — accept or reject

The list view is my proposal. The document describes the authoring flow in detail and the registry that holds the output, but not how an author finds an existing definition to clone or version.

L2 · Configuration Work Definition Author Author · one project Web console Live in the demo — the one shipped fix

The counting basis fork — the most consequential question in the product

On screen: Work Definition Author

Is this work counted by event, by time, or by outcome? A category and a discrete unit are only asked when the answer is event.

Why it works this way

Category and unit used to be mandatory with no escape hatch, so a salaried Anganwadi worker, a health extension worker, a sanitation wage and a contract teacher all had to force themselves into a category that did not fit. Asking the fork first means a salaried role is never asked for a unit at all.

Assumption — accept or reject

None on the fork itself — this is specified and shipped. What is mine is showing the consequence of each choice on the card, so an author can see why the question matters.

What the system does here

Work Definition Registry & Versioning Service
Persists counting basis as the field that determines which downstream fields exist at all.

L2 · Configuration Work Definition Author Author · one project Web console Proposed, built nowhere

A training cascade is a chain of linked definitions

On screen: Work Definition Author

A role level on the definition, plus a reference to the definition one level up. Three levels of a training cascade become three linked records rather than one overloaded one.

Why it works this way

A binary trainee-or-trainer field cannot hold a three-level cascade. A master trainer who trains trainers who train workers is three distinct pieces of work, each with its own evidence and its own rate.

Assumption — accept or reject

Everything here is proposed. Two things are undecided and both matter: whether the chain is validated at all — can a level-three definition exist with no level two? — and whether a trainer’s credential should carry the outcomes of the people they trained.

L2 · Configuration Work Definition Author Author · one project Web console Live, with paired proof proposed

What proves it happened, tier by tier

On screen: Work Definition Author

The evidence acceptable at each tier, the highest tier available for this work type, and how intensively evidence is checked. This is the face of the definition a worker reads before starting.

Why it works this way

The tier ceiling is declared here, and a credential can never be issued above it. Declaring Tier 2 as the ceiling for community mobilisation tells a verifier that Tier 1 was structurally unavailable — the worker did not fall short of anything.

Assumption — accept or reject

The paired-proof option — a required before-and-after photo — is a proposal. Proof types are flat labels today and cannot hold a structured pair.

Source · 7 of 9

Where does this evidence come from?

Pick how records of this work will reach CREST. Every option is somewhere else: CREST reads or receives, and never records. You can add more than one later, and the lowest-trust source in use caps the tier.

A system CREST connects toTier 1 available
An adaptor pulls records in on a schedule. Nobody retypes anything, which is the only way Tier 1 is reachable.
A spreadsheet the team uploadsTier 2 ceiling
You get a template generated from this definition. Sensible where the work happens outside any system.
A worker typing it into CRESTTier 3 ceiling
Does not exist. CREST has no screen on which work is recorded, because evidence CREST captured itself would be CREST vouching for its own record.
A supervisor confirming in the delivery platform’s own appTier 2 ceiling
A named person vouches for it. Already covered by the attestation rule on the previous step.
Why this matters
Whatever you choose here, the evidence rules you just set still apply. The source decides the highest tier that is structurally possible; the rules decide whether a given record reaches it.
L2 · Configuration Work Definition Author Author · one project Web console

The choice that caps the trust tier

On screen: Work Definition Author

Before a definition can be ratified, it has to say where the record of the work will actually arrive from. This is the field the Matching engine reads to decide whether it can clear anything automatically.

Why it works this way

This one answer sets the ceiling on everything downstream. A spreadsheet that a person types cannot support Tier 1, no matter what the evidence rules say, because somebody retyped it. Choosing the source is therefore not an implementation detail — it decides what a credential from this definition can ever claim.

Open — not decided

The tier a source can support is currently inferred from the source type. Whether an accredited adaptor should raise that ceiling, and an unaccredited one cap it, is not decided.

A template the definition writes for you

On screen: Work Definition Author

The columns, their types and their allowed values are generated from this work definition — not chosen here. Anything the definition requires becomes a required column, and the unit of work becomes the quantity column.

Why it works this way

Handing someone a blank spreadsheet guarantees a mismatch between what they send and what the definition expects. Generating it from the definition removes the guesswork, and means a rejected upload is a data problem rather than a format argument.

Open — not decided

A template is generated per definition version. An upload made against v1.1 after v1.2 is published will be rejected, and nothing currently warns the uploader that their file is out of date.

The adaptor library, and what is missing from it

On screen: Work Definition Author

A class adaptor knows the shape of one kind of source system and translates it into CREST’s own fields. Five are built against real published contracts. Three more are named because the shape is understood, but nothing behind them exists yet.

Why it works this way

Without adaptors, every integration is bespoke and every partner negotiates the same field names again. An adaptor makes the translation a reusable, reviewable thing — and makes it obvious when a source is a shape nobody has handled before.

Open — not decided

Whether an adaptor carries an accreditation of its own, so that a vetted adaptor can support Tier 1 and a hand-built one cannot, is proposed and not decided.

L2 · Configuration Work Definition Author Author · one project Web console

Where an integration actually gets hard

On screen: Work Definition Author

The adaptor proposes what it can match by name and type. What it cannot match is the interesting part: this source has no field for the unit this definition counts.

Why it works this way

A mapping that leaves a required field empty cannot go live, and saying so here rather than at the first failed run is the difference between a configuration step and a support ticket. The unmatched row is not a bug in the adaptor — the source system genuinely does not record what this definition pays for.

Open — not decided

Deriving a quantity from a count of related records is proposed. Whether CREST should host expressions like that at all, or insist the source system provides the number, is not decided.

Connection details, and the credential CREST never sees

On screen: Work Definition Author

Where to reach the system, how often, and which records are in scope. The credential itself is not entered here and is not stored in the definition.

Why it works this way

Whoever authors a work definition is rarely the person who holds the partner’s API credential, and should not have to be. Separating the two means the definition can be finished and reviewed without waiting on a secret, and the secret never sits in a record that other organisations can read.

Open — not decided

Where the credential does live is unresolved. Key and secret custody has no confirmed owner anywhere in the project, and this screen is one of the places that gap shows.

L2 · Configuration Work Definition Author Author · one project Web console Proposed, not built anywhere

Stacked pay, tranches, and a rate that varies by item

On screen: Rate Owner (F-1)

Pay basis, rate structure and rate value fold into each payment tranche rather than sitting on the parent record. A single-trigger definition becomes the one-tranche case.

Why it works this way

The flat shape could not hold a fixed fee plus a piece-rate bonus together, a commission on value, a clawback if treatment was abandoned, a warranty holdback, or a rate that varies by material rather than by volume. Seven of the twenty first-round failures concentrated here.

Assumption — accept or reject

Everything on this screen is proposed and built nowhere. Tranches, rateTable, threshold-bearing triggers and clawback direction are each a separate decision. Drawing them together is my attempt to show whether they cohere as one interface — they may not.

L2 · Configuration Work Definition Author Author · one project Web console Half live — new values yes, new fields no

Two kinds of extension, with very different costs

On screen: Work Definition Author

A new value in an existing slot is free and immediate. A genuinely new field the schema never anticipated needs its own mechanism, modelled on FHIR’s extension pattern, with keys namespaced to whoever invented them.

Why it works this way

The two look the same to the person filling in the form and are not the same at all. A new category name costs nothing. A contractor reference number is only understood by whatever screen was built to read that specific key, so two institutions solving the same problem under two different keys will not compare.

Assumption — accept or reject

The new-value path is live. extensionFields[] is proposed and built nowhere. Keeping both on one screen, without leaving the form, is the stated direction — but it does mean showing the author a cost they may not care about.

What the system does here
S-5
Work Definition Registry & Versioning Service
Stores an institution extension as its own independently versioned layer.

L2 · Configuration Work Definition Author Author · one project Schema Mixed — see each field

What the record actually is, underneath the form

On screen: Architect view — not a screen an author sees

A work definition is two layers. A base schema every institution shares, with identical meaning everywhere, and an institution extension holding whatever one institution needs for its own operational reality.

Why it works this way

The shared base is what lets two institutions’ definitions be compared or trusted against each other. The extension is what stops that shared core from having to absorb every local field, so it can change rarely and only network-wide.

Assumption — accept or reject

Putting the schema in front of you is my choice — an author never sees this. It is here because the audience for this prototype includes an architect, and the form only makes sense once you can see what it writes.

Open questions
Work Definition Author — six unresolved
Open questions6

Six open questions

How does a group payment split back to individuals?
Needs a formula or reference object, not another field. Blocks cooperative and gang-based work outright.
Blocking
Who governs promoting an institution-invented field into shared vocabulary?
Centrally by whoever runs the network, or negotiated peer-to-peer between the institutions reusing it?
Blocking
How is validation delegation implemented?
Reuse the existing standing-role invite mechanism, or build a one-off delegation tied to a single definition? They model different things.
Design
Can a role hold more than one counting basis?
A peer mental-health worker on a retainer plus per-session pay feels like one role. Is the honest answer two linked definitions?
Design
Should sector ever hard-filter categories?
Deliberately left as a suggestion, because a hard filter would make the sectors with no matching category worse, not better.
Settled for now
When do the proposed schema extensions get built?
No owner, no date. A sequencing decision, not a design one.
Unowned
One case is not a gap at all but a boundary worth naming: a tour guide’s stipend is fully representable, and their cash tips are outside any system by design. Pretending otherwise would be worse than stating the limit.
What happens next
What just happenedThe work definition is signed and active · WD-4471 v1.2
Who acts nextWorkers, supervisors and the systems that feed it
WhenLive immediately; the first records usually arrive within the hour
How you will be toldA notice to everyone assigned to this project
If nothing happens · If nothing arrives within a day, the source is probably not connected. Check the connection screen.

Checks Tier 2 and Tier 3 evidence against the Work Definition; views the resolved evidence tier. Acceptance here is what causes the credential to be issued — there is no separate human signing step. A template out, a file back

On screen: External Evidence Contact — county training institute

An external institution supplies attestation evidence into a work unit — the reverse direction from a verifier, who consumes credentials rather than feeding them.

Why it works this way

Some work is best evidenced by a third party that is neither the employer nor the worker. A training institute confirming a course completion is independent in a way a supervisor cannot be.

Assumption — accept or reject

This role is classed as supporting, not blocking, and has no value bundle. Everything here is proposed: the request model, the single-event scope, and the idea that the institution never gets a standing account.

The value is the independence, so the submission has to carry the institution’s identity. An unsigned confirmation is worth no more than the worker’s own assertion.

On screen: Rate Owner — invited by email

Credentials are unaffected. Work validated from today issues credentials normally; they simply carry no payment yet. A project that never completes this half is still a working project.
What happens next
What just happenedThe rate is set and applies from the next cycle · RATE-118-03

What is now owed, and by whom
Setting a rate does not make money move. Three things are outstanding, each owed by exactly one party, and each will sit quietly until somebody acts:
The pathway — owed by whoever owns the payment mechanism. Until it is set, cleared work produces no instruction at all.
The settlement account — owed by the payment organisation. Until it is proved, instructions are made but nothing is sent.
The finance code — owed by the project. Until it is linked, payments cannot post to anybody’s books.
None of these escalates on its own. Each appears as an open item on the project until it is closed.

Where does CREST’s job end for this project?

One question. Everything after it follows from the answer.

At a payment advisory
CREST works out what is owed and issues a statement. Somebody else pays it.
· No rail, no credentials, no integration
· CREST never learns whether it was paid
· Right where you already have a finance system
At a payment instruction
CREST raises the instruction and follows it to whatever carries the money.
· You choose one or more rails next
· Confirmation comes back, so reconciliation is possible
· Right where you want CREST to close the loop
This is not a choice between four payment methods. It is a choice about where CREST stops. Methods only exist on one side of it.
L2 · ConfigurationPayment Mechanism Owner Author · one projectOne console · payment set upThe one fork

Where CREST stops, not how it pays

On screen: Payment Mechanism Owner — Malaria Bednet Campaign

The first question is how far CREST goes: does it stop at telling you what is owed, or does it go on to raise the instruction and follow it? Payment methods are a second question, and only on one branch.

Why it works this way

Advisory is not a lesser rail — it is a different end point. An organisation with its own finance system and no appetite to connect it gets full calculation, full traceability and no integration. Ranking it alongside bank transfers would misrepresent what it is.

Assumption — accept or reject

Framing this as one fork rather than a list of methods is my proposal. The architecture establishes both postures; it does not say which question is asked first, and asking it the other way round is what made the earlier version confusing.

What the system does here
S-14
Payment Calculation Engine
Runs on both branches. What is owed is calculated either way.

Payment Trigger & Routing Engine
Only wakes on the instruction branch.

L2 · ConfigurationPayment Mechanism Owner Author · one projectOne console · payment set upMulti-select

One project, several rails

On screen: Payment Mechanism Owner — choosing rails

A worker with a bank account and a worker with only a phone cannot be paid the same way. Forcing one rail per project would exclude whichever group the project picked against.

Why it works this way

Routing is per worker, not per project: the rail follows the payout details the worker actually gave. That is only possible if a project can hold more than one rail at once.

Assumption — accept or reject

Multi-select is my proposal, and it raises a question nothing answers: what happens to a worker whose details fit none of the chosen rails. Today they would simply never be paid, silently.

Proving the whole path, once

On screen: Payment Mechanism Owner — rail setup, step 2

One small payment to an account the operator controls, tracked all the way through to CREST reading the confirmation back. Four states, each of which can fail independently.

Why it works this way

Every one of these four lines is a different failure. Raised but not accepted is a credential problem; accepted but not confirmed is a rail problem; confirmed but not read back is a reconciliation problem. Collapsing them into one tick would hide which is which.

Assumption — accept or reject

The whole result is simulated. What a real test costs — a live account, a real transfer, a reversal path — is not modelled, and no rail is actually contacted.

A statement, and an honest limit

On screen: Payment Mechanism Owner — advisory template

The advisory pathway needs no integration and no credentials. What it needs is agreement on what the statement contains, and clarity that CREST never learns whether it was acted on.

Why it works this way

This is the pathway for an organisation with its own finance system and no appetite to connect it. Making the last row explicit — that CREST cannot say whether anything was paid — is what stops the statement being mistaken for a receipt.

Assumption — accept or reject

The statement contents are my proposal. The architecture establishes advisory as a real posture; it does not specify what a statement contains, how it is delivered, or whether a worker ever sees one.

When is a payment raised?

What starts the clock, and how often the money actually goes out.

As soon as a work unit is validated
Each validated event raises its own instruction. Fastest for the worker, most instructions for the rail.
Batched weekly
Validated events accumulate and go out together each Friday.
Batched monthly
One run a month. Cheapest to operate, slowest for the worker.
Hold payment if a dispute is open
Yes
A disputed work unit does not pay until the Grievance Manager (Grievance Manager) resolves it.
Manual approval before release
Off
On sends every payment to a Payment Approver (Payment Approver) first.
Batching is a cost decision made by the project and paid for by the worker. A monthly run means a worker who finishes today waits up to thirty days.
L2 · ConfigurationPayment Mechanism Owner Author · one projectOne console · payment set up

Batching is paid for by the worker

On screen: Payment Mechanism Owner — trigger and timing

Three timings that differ mainly in who absorbs the inconvenience. Per-event is best for the worker and most expensive to run; monthly is the reverse.

Why it works this way

The roles master gives this role the trigger and timing alongside the pathway, because they are the same decision in practice: what a rail costs per instruction is usually what drives the batching choice.

Assumption — accept or reject

Naming the worker-side cost of batching is mine, and it is a nudge. The dispute hold is drawn from the architecture; whether it should be configurable at all is arguable, since paying out a disputed event is hard to undo.

What the system does here
S-20
Payment Trigger & Routing Engine
Fires instructions on whichever trigger is set here.
S-15
Aggregation Engine
Groups events into a run under either batching option.

What is now owed, and by whom
Setting a rate does not make money move. Three things are outstanding, each owed by exactly one party, and each will sit quietly until somebody acts:
The pathway — owed by whoever owns the payment mechanism. Until it is set, cleared work produces no instruction at all.
The settlement account — owed by the payment organisation. Until it is proved, instructions are made but nothing is sent.
The finance code — owed by the project. Until it is linked, payments cannot post to anybody’s books.
None of these escalates on its own. Each appears as an open item on the project until it is closed.

Configured is not the same as live

On screen: Payment Mechanism Owner — review

Why it works this way

Keeping activation separate from completion is the same principle as the project itself activating with gaps: finishing a form should never be what starts real money moving.

Assumption — accept or reject

The sandbox-to-live step is my proposal and it is not designed. Who may flip it, whether it requires a second person, and what happens to instructions raised in sandbox are all unspecified.

On screen: Worker — Amara Kimani

The campaign ends, the source system data is fetched, and a draft credential is created. The worker has seven days to confirm or dispute. Silence auto-confirms on day seven.

Auto-confirmation is load-bearing. Without it an unclaimed credential blocks payment indefinitely, and the workers most likely to be unreachable are the most vulnerable ones.

Assumption — accept or reject

Showing a countdown is my addition. The architecture specifies the window and the auto-confirm behaviour, not whether the worker sees time remaining. A countdown may create pressure; consider testing it.

Raising a dispute

On screen: Worker → Grievance Manager (P-7) (P-10)

The worker states what is wrong. The issuer has 14 days to respond and correct; if they do not, the system defaults in the worker’s favour.

The 14-day default is the single strongest worker protection in the architecture. It inverts the usual asymmetry: silence from an institution helps the worker rather than exhausting them.

Assumption — accept or reject

Pre-set dispute reasons are my proposal, so the case arrives classified. The architecture specifies the window, the burden of proof and the default, not the intake form.

A month, not a job at a time

On screen: Worker — Amara Kimani

Four jobs in August across two wards and two employers, with what has arrived, what has cleared but not been sent, and what is still being checked. One of them pays nothing and is shown anyway, because being recognised for work is a separate thing from being paid for it.

Why it works this way

A worker holding four jobs in a month cannot plan from four separate payment screens. The question they actually have is how much is coming and when, and that only answers itself when the jobs are added together. Splitting cleared-but-unpaid from still-being-checked matters because those two wait on completely different people.

Open — not decided

There is no forecast here. A worker planning a month wants to know when the eight thousand arrives, and nothing in this product currently commits to a date it could show.

Why money has not arrived, and whose problem it is

On screen: Worker — Amara Kimani

Two held amounts, each with the reason and the named party. One passed its check and is simply waiting for somebody to raise the payment. The other is held because the records arrived naming a superseded version of the definition. Neither is the worker’s to fix, and the screen says so twice.

Why it works this way

This is the same held-record list the project sees, turned around and shown to the person the money belongs to. A worker who is told only that a payment is pending has no way to tell a slow week from a stuck record, and no way to know whether chasing is worth it. Naming the office and the number of days does both. It also removes the worst outcome, which is a worker assuming they did something wrong.

Open — not decided

Whether a worker should be able to chase directly from here, rather than through a support agent, is undecided. It would be more useful and it puts a named district officer’s workload at the mercy of several hundred workers.

Consent, per share, every time

On screen: Worker — Amara Kimani

A verifier asks to see the record. The worker approves that specific request, and chooses what it discloses. What the verifier can resolve is bounded by what the worker approves here, and by nothing else — there is no accreditation status that widens it.

Why it works this way

Selective disclosure is a layer of the architecture, not a setting. Any third party can verify a credential without onboarding to CREST, because the credential's own signature carries the trust. That only stays safe if the worker, not the verifier, decides how much is revealed at each share.

Assumption — accept or reject

A field-by-field disclosure choice is my proposal. The role model establishes that consent at share time is the control; it does not specify the granularity the worker is offered, or whether a worker can save a preset for repeat verifiers.

What the system does here
S-12
Consent Management & Access Control Service
Enforces this per-share choice — this is the control point the whole verifier model rests on.
S-11
Provenance / Audit Logging Service
Logs who verified what, and when.

The Registering Agent’s day starts with a list

On screen: Registering Agent — Mary Wambui

A field agent registering workers who cannot or do not self-register. The app works offline and syncs later.

Pathway B exists for workers with no phone or low literacy. It is assigned by an Org Admin and audited by agent ID, so an assisted registration is always traceable to a named person.

Assumption — accept or reject

A queue of expected registrations is my proposal. The architecture describes the enrollment act, not how an agent finds who to enroll — in practice this may be a walk-up desk with no list at all.

The agent reads the consent form aloud in the local language. The worker confirms verbally and the voice consent is recorded, timestamped and tied to the agent’s ID.

A signature from someone who cannot read the form is not consent. Voice consent in the worker’s own language, with the agent named, is the architecture’s answer and it is the audit trail as well.

Assumption — accept or reject

A script displayed for the agent to read verbatim is my addition — it is what makes the recording comparable across agents. Language selection and script wording need legal review per jurisdiction.

Tier 2 evidence is only as timely as the supervisor. A pull model makes the worker wait on someone else remembering; a pushed list with a visible clock does not.

Assumption — accept or reject

The countdown against each worker is my addition. The 48-hour window in batch claiming is specified; showing it as per-worker urgency is a design decision that shapes behaviour.

Confirming inside the system that recorded it

On screen: Supervisor — Samuel Otieno

The supervisor works in the platform that recorded the delivery, not in CREST. They see what it recorded and confirm or correct it there, and the confirmation reaches CREST as part of the same record on the next pull.

Why it works this way

The architecture names the risk in Tier 2 directly: the issuer has authority but also bias, and supervisor-worker collusion is the primary failure mode. Naming the signer is the countermeasure.

Assumption — accept or reject

Showing the source system’s own count alongside the worker’s is my proposal — it turns a blank attestation into a comparison. Whether supervisors should be able to see and override the machine count needs a policy decision.

Two of three, and the old key dies

On screen: System — recovery threshold met

Once two nominees confirm, a new key is issued and linked to the full credential history. The original key is cryptographically invalidated.

Why it works this way

Credentials issued under the old key stay valid — the history is not lost. But no new credential can be issued under it, which closes the window on a stolen handset.

Assumption — accept or reject

Telling the nominee the outcome is my addition. Without it they have replied into silence and have no way to know whether they helped or were phished.

X-2

Instance Registry Maintainer

Instance
DEFINITION ONLY — SCREENS NOT DRAWN

Keeps the instance's skill code list current.

Decides what enters any shared definition at instance level, then keeps each one versioned and published: the credential format's CREST-specific parts, the Work Definition template library, the instance's adoption of the shared skill list, and whether an external source system may supply evidence at all. One act applied to several assets: decide what enters a shared definition, then version and publish it. The assets stay distinct; the accountability does not need to. Certifying a source system sits here rather than with Platform Operations (X-1), so that whoever builds an integration is never the person who approves it.

What this role covers
  • Adopts and publishes the shared skill list held at the platform release, and forwards proposals for new codes to it.
  • Keeps the instance's credential format up to date — updates fields as they change, and publishes new versions so credentials stay readable. The format is a W3C Verifiable Credential; this role owns the CREST-specific parts of it and the context that defines them.
  • Curates a library of ready-to-use Work Definition templates a Work Definition Author can start from.
  • Reviews requests for new Work Definition templates when nothing in the library fits, and adds new ones as needed.
  • Accredits a class adapter — one per system class, so every DHIS2 or CommCare deployment connects by configuration rather than engineering — and separately approves a one-off source that has no class adapter behind it. Reviews and certifies whether an external source system is trustworthy enough to supply evidence. Two things to check: does its data map to what the Work Definition expects, and do its terms mean the same thing as CREST's (e.g. that its 'household covered' means CREST's 'household visited').
  • Approves the join key for each source system — how that system's own worker identifier resolves to a Crest identity. It is the most failure-prone field in the whole evidence path: get it wrong and work is credited to the wrong person, or to nobody.

V-1

Verifier

External
Step 1 of 3
New journeyJourney 11 of 12Checking a credential

Any third party checking a credential with no relationship to CREST at all — someone scanning a QR code at a hiring desk, a lender, an inspector. Sees the base disclosure: verified or not, how many campaigns, and the skill codes held. Needs no account, no onboarding, and no connectivity beyond resolving the credential. What a verifier sees is the narrower of two things: the accreditation level they hold, and what the worker consented to disclose for that share. Neither alone decides it. An unaccredited verifier cannot be granted more by consent than their level allows, and an accredited one still sees only what the worker approved.

No CREST onboarding required

What a pass lets you see
With a pass you will see: whether the credential is valid, the skill it names, the trust tier it was issued at, and how many times work was validated. You will not see the worker’s name, identity number, phone, location, employer, or any individual record.

L3 · Product Verifier no role — a pass, not an account Web console

Identified, but not onboarded

On screen: Verifier

Anyone can check a CREST credential. What they cannot do is check one anonymously. A pass takes a verified email or phone, a name, and a stated reason — no organisation, no accreditation, no vetting.

Why it works this way

The worker is the one being examined, so the worker gets to know who examined them. Making the verifier identifiable costs them thirty seconds and gives the worker an audit trail they can actually read. Anonymous checking would have been simpler and would have quietly inverted whose interests the system serves.

Open — not decided

Nothing stops someone taking a pass under a false name. The pass proves an email was reachable, not that a person is who they say — and the disclosure limits are set accordingly.

Institutional Verifier

External
Step 1 of 3
New journeyJourney 11 of 12Checking a credential

A verifier that has onboarded and holds an accreditation level, so it resolves more than an anonymous scan: campaign names, issuing organisations and dates at the registered level; full credential detail, including the definitions and evidence behind each claim, at the institutional level. Where a Payment Set Up is attached, an institutional verifier with consent can additionally resolve what the work was priced at and whether it was paid. Enters through the same Onboarding Authorising Signatory step as any other accountable organisation, then branches at recognition, where its criteria differ: a verifier issues nothing, so what it is granted is a disclosure level rather than authority to attest. Still bounded by worker consent at every share.

Where volume becomes a different question

On screen: Institutional Verifier · Equity Bank

An institution can check a list. Each row still needs its own consent, which means a batch is not one decision but four hundred, and it completes over hours or days rather than seconds.

Why it works this way

Batching is the honest way to serve a bank opening four hundred accounts. Making each row need its own consent is what stops it becoming a bulk export of a worker registry — the friction is the safeguard, not a shortcoming.

Open — not decided

No rule limits how many batches an institution may run, or requires it to state a purpose per batch rather than per check. This is the clearest place the model is thin.
