L3 · Product Funding Oversight Viewer · Global Fund Reviewer + Verifier · a portfolio of projects Web console

Allocated against paid, and the gap in between

On screen: Funding Oversight Viewer · Global Fund

A funder does not want a project dashboard six times. They want the portfolio, ranked by where money is sitting still.

Why it works this way

The number a funder is accountable for is not spend, it is unspent — money committed to work that has not happened, or work that has happened and has not been paid for. Both are visible here and neither is visible on a single project view.

Open — not decided

Nothing reconciles a funder’s own ledger against what CREST reports. These figures are CREST’s, and a funder will reasonably ask why they differ from theirs.

Follow the tier column
Loima is the whole problem. Its counselling sessions are Tier 2, which routes every record to a validator, and the project named one validator for five sub-counties. The money is not blocked by a payment fault — it is blocked by a staffing decision made at setup.

L3 · Product Funding Oversight Viewer · Global Fund Reviewer + Verifier · a portfolio of projects Web console

From an amount to a place, a service and a day

On screen: Funding Oversight Viewer · Global Fund

One project, opened. Money by sub-county, then by work definition, then to the individual validated records behind a payment — without ever naming a worker.

Why it works this way

A funder’s assurance question is whether the money bought the work it was meant to buy. Answering it needs geography, service type and dates. It does not need identities, and a view that supplies them anyway creates an obligation the funder never asked for.

Open — not decided

Aggregation to sub-county is a choice, not a rule. In a sparsely staffed ward, four records and a service type can identify a worker as effectively as a name.

L3 · ProductS-4 · Identity Anchor (Layer 0)External system · phoneNot operated by CREST

Where identity actually comes from

On screen: National ID service — the anchor CREST binds to

CREST never creates an identity. The worker authenticates against whatever the country already runs — a national ID service, mobile OTP, or MOSIP — and CREST receives an assertion that the person is who they claim to be.

Why it works this way

Layer 0 is explicitly not owned by CREST. Binding to an existing anchor rather than minting a new identity is what stops CREST becoming yet another parallel registry a worker has to maintain.

Assumption — accept or reject

This screen is entirely illustrative. Every country’s anchor looks different, and what a real one returns — a token, an assertion, a full record — determines how much CREST ever holds. Whether the ID number itself is stored is a decision this drawing assumes away.

What the system does here
S-4
Identity Anchor System (Layer 0) · external
This screen is that service. CREST calls it and receives an assertion.
S-1
Identity Resolution & Linking Service
Takes the assertion and links it to a Crest identity, creating one only if none exists.

L3 · ProductS-7 · Service Delivery PlatformExternal system · web consoleTier 1 origin

Where the strongest evidence is recorded

On screen: DIGIT HCM — a campaign delivery system

Tier 1 evidence originates outside CREST, in whatever system already records service delivery. Its strength comes from the fact that neither the worker nor the supervisor entered it.

Why it works this way

The tier hierarchy is about who had the opportunity to inflate the record. A campaign system logging a household visit has no stake in how many visits a particular CHW is credited with, which is what makes it stronger than a supervisor’s attestation.

Assumption — accept or reject

The specific fields are illustrative of a DIGIT HCM-style record rather than drawn from its actual contract. The semantic-equivalence problem the second note raises is real and unresolved: the roles master gives X-3 that judgment but nothing specifies how a mismatch is recorded.

What the system does here
S-7
Service Delivery Platform · external
This screen is that system. The record exists here first.
S-6
Evidence Intake Adapter
Pulls this record into CREST through the accredited adapter for this system class — one adapter serves every deployment of it. A source with no class adapter can still be added one-off, approved on its own terms.
S-8
Matching / Validation Engine
Matches it against the work definition to resolve the tier.

L3 · ProductS-21 · Bank / FSP / MNOExternal system · console + the worker’s SMSMoney moves here

The boundary where CREST stops

On screen: A payment rail executing a batch, and what the worker receives

CREST calculates, raises one instruction per validated work unit, and tracks status. The rail is what actually moves money, and the worker usually learns about it from the rail first.

Why it works this way

One instruction per work unit rather than one per batch is what makes a single failure recoverable without disturbing 411 other payments, and what keeps every payment traceable back to the event that earned it.

Assumption — accept or reject

Showing the worker’s SMS beside the rail console is a deliberate choice. The consistency problem it raises is real and unaddressed: if the SMS says paid and CREST says pending, nothing currently specifies which the worker should believe or how the gap is closed.

What the system does here
S-20
Payment Trigger & Routing Engine
Raised these instructions and routed them to this rail.
S-21
Bank / FSP System · external
This screen. The only place money actually moves.
S-22
Payment Status Tracking Engine
Reads sent, confirmed, failed and pending back from here.
S-24
Reconciliation Engine
Compares what was calculated against what this rail confirms, and flags the difference.

L3 · ProductVerifier no role — a pass, not an accountExternal system · the employer’s own consoleNo CREST onboarding

Why the credential is worth anything

On screen: A next employer checking a claim inside their own hiring system

This is the point of the whole system. An employer with no relationship to CREST can confirm 14 months of validated work in seconds, and the worker decided exactly how much of it they could see.

Why it works this way

Verifiers deliberately do not onboard. Requiring accreditation would make the credential only as portable as CREST’s own reach, when the signature already makes it verifiable anywhere. Trust comes from the credential, not from the checker’s status.

Assumption — accept or reject

This screen is drawn as an employer’s own system rather than a CREST portal, which is a real assumption. In practice most small employers would use a hosted verifier page; showing it embedded makes the point about portability, but overstates how integrated a first deployment would be.

What the system does here
S-12

Decided every line on this screen — including the two withheld ones.
